7|Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network|"# Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network

This community centers on renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, and its metastatic spread. Key entities include RCC, its sarcomatoid variant (sRCC), various subtypes (ccRCC, clear cell papillary RCC, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, ELOC-mutated RCC), and distant sites of metastasis such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The relationships illustrate how RCC can transform into sarcomatoid RCC, how metastasis occurs to these sites, and how physical exams can detect lymph node involvement.

## RCC is the most common kidney cancer with high metastatic potential

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, originating in the renal tubules. It has a high propensity to metastasize, as evidenced by multiple relationships linking RCC to distant sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The centrality of RCC is underscored by its high degree (8) and its connections to various subtypes. The metastatic capability makes RCC a significant clinical challenge, as early detection and treatment are critical for patient outcomes. [Data: Entities (25, 48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46); Relationships (49, 56, 55, 57, 58, 59)]

## Sarcomatoid RCC is an aggressive variant arising from any RCC subtype

Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) is a highly aggressive form of kidney cancer that can arise from almost any type of RCC, as indicated by the relationship between sRCC and RCC. This transformation is associated with a worse prognosis and increased likelihood of metastasis. sRCC occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors but tends to grow and spread more rapidly. The entity 'SRCC' is synonymous with sarcomatoid RCC, highlighting the importance of recognizing this variant due to its clinical implications. [Data: Entities (39, 40); Relationships (47, 48)]

## Metastasis is a central process involving multiple distant sites

Metastasis is a key process in kidney cancer progression, where cancer cells travel through blood or lymph to form new tumors outside the kidney. The data reveals that RCC commonly metastasizes to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. This pattern of spread guides staging and treatment decisions. The high degree of the metastasis entity (9) and its numerous relationships underscore its critical role in the disease. [Data: Entities (48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46, 64); Relationships (56, 55, 57, 58, 59, 76)]

## Clear cell RCC is the most common subtype, with several recently defined subtypes

Clear cell RCC (ccRCC) is the predominant subtype of RCC, accounting for about 70% of cases. Additionally, several recently defined RCC types have been identified, including clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC. These subtypes have distinct molecular and pathological features that may influence prognosis and treatment. The relationships show that these subtypes are all connected to RCC, indicating their classification within the broader RCC spectrum. [Data: Entities (26, 36, 37, 38); Relationships (33, 44, 45, 46)]

## Lymph nodes are key sites for metastasis and physical examination

Lymph nodes serve as an important site for kidney cancer metastasis and are also accessible during physical exams. Enlarged lymph nodes in areas such as the neck, underarm, and groin can be felt by healthcare providers, potentially indicating disease involvement. This dual role—as a metastatic site and a clinical indicator—makes lymph nodes a critical entity in the assessment and staging of kidney cancer. The relationship between physical exam and lymph nodes highlights the clinical utility of this examination. [Data: Entities (43, 109); Relationships (56, 142)]

## The primary tumor and metastatic tumors are interconnected in disease progression

The primary tumor is the original tumor in the kidney from which cancer cells can spread. Metastatic tumors form when cancer cells from the primary tumor travel to distant sites. Understanding this relationship is essential for understanding the natural history of kidney cancer and for developing treatment strategies. The data explicitly links metastasis to both the primary tumor and metastatic tumors, emphasizing the continuum of disease progression. [Data: Entities (65, 64); Relationships (77, 76)]"

These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait and sickle cell disease, particularly in young people of African descent. Collecting duct RCC forms in the collecting ducts and is also known as cdRCC. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by chromophobe cells. The community highlights the diversity of NCCRCC and its connections to specific cellular features and genetic conditions.

## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

## The community highlights the importance of accurate subtyping for prognosis and treatment

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. The structured relationships in this community provide a framework for classifying and studying NCCRCC. [Data: Entities (27, 34, 21, 29, 32); Relationships (34, 42, 21, 37, 40, +more)]"

Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These hormones control metabolism, blood pressure, and body features (such as hair growth and body shape). Adrenal medulla – This is the inner part of the adrenal gland. The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. Adrenal glands Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed three-dimensional (3D) picture. In most cases, contrast will be used. Contrast Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. Contrast is used to make the pictures clearer. It might be taken by mouth (oral) or given through a vein (IV). The contrast is not permanent and will leave the body in your urine after the test. The types of contrast vary but are different for CT than for MRI. Tell your doctors if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and prednisone (steroids), to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys are not working well. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Contrast might be used. An MRI may be used as an initial test, to check treatment results, and to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. PET scans are performed about an hour after the tracer is injected. PET scans are combined with CT or MRI scans (PET/CT or PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. This combined test is considered to be more accurate than either scan alone. Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. 0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. Adrenal glands produce hormones that affect your body in different ways. This chapter reviews the basics of adrenal tumors. Adrenal glands Your body has 2 adrenal glands. They are located on top of each kidney. Adrenal glands are small, yellow glands that are important to the body’s endocrine system. The endocrine system is made up of tissues and organs that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These hormones control metabolism, blood pressure, and body features (such as hair growth and body shape). Adrenal medulla – This is the inner part of the adrenal gland. The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. Adrenal glands Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. Adrenal tumors often do not cause symptoms and are found through an imaging test such as a CT or MRI scan performed for another reason. Benign functional tumors can still produce hormones and may be found during tests for hormone-related symptoms. Malignant adrenal tumors are cancerous tumors. The community centers on Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC), a category of kidney cancers distinct from clear cell RCC. Key entities include various subtypes: papillary RCC (the most common), chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, collecting duct RCC, and renal medullary carcinoma. These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. Collecting duct RCC forms in the collecting ducts and is also known as cdRCC. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by chromophobe cells. ## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. ## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. ## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

## The community highlights the importance of accurate subtyping for prognosis and treatment

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. This community centers on renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, and its metastatic spread. Key entities include RCC, its sarcomatoid variant (sRCC), various subtypes (ccRCC, clear cell papillary RCC, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, ELOC-mutated RCC), and distant sites of metastasis such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The relationships illustrate how RCC can transform into sarcomatoid RCC, how metastasis occurs to these sites, and how physical exams can detect lymph node involvement.

## RCC is the most common kidney cancer with high metastatic potential

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, originating in the renal tubules. It has a high propensity to metastasize, as evidenced by multiple relationships linking RCC to distant sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The centrality of RCC is underscored by its high degree (8) and its connections to various subtypes. The metastatic capability makes RCC a significant clinical challenge, as early detection and treatment are critical for patient outcomes. [Data: Entities (25, 48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46); Relationships (49, 56, 55, 57, 58, 59)]

## Sarcomatoid RCC is an aggressive variant arising from any RCC subtype

Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) is a highly aggressive form of kidney cancer that can arise from almost any type of RCC, as indicated by the relationship between sRCC and RCC. This transformation is associated with a worse prognosis and increased likelihood of metastasis. sRCC occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors but tends to grow and spread more rapidly. The entity 'SRCC' is synonymous with sarcomatoid RCC, highlighting the importance of recognizing this variant due to its clinical implications. [Data: Entities (39, 40); Relationships (47, 48)]

## Metastasis is a central process involving multiple distant sites

Metastasis is a key process in kidney cancer progression, where cancer cells travel through blood or lymph to form new tumors outside the kidney. The data reveals that RCC commonly metastasizes to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. This pattern of spread guides staging and treatment decisions. The high degree of the metastasis entity (9) and its numerous relationships underscore its critical role in the disease. [Data: Entities (48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46, 64); Relationships (56, 55, 57, 58, 59, 76)]

## Clear cell RCC is the most common subtype, with several recently defined subtypes

Clear cell RCC (ccRCC) is the predominant subtype of RCC, accounting for about 70% of cases. Additionally, several recently defined RCC types have been identified, including clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC. These subtypes have distinct molecular and pathological features that may influence prognosis and treatment. The relationships show that these subtypes are all connected to RCC, indicating their classification within the broader RCC spectrum. [Data: Entities (26, 36, 37, 38); Relationships (33, 44, 45, 46)]

## Lymph nodes are key sites for metastasis and physical examination

Lymph nodes serve as an important site for kidney cancer metastasis and are also accessible during physical exams. Enlarged lymph nodes in areas such as the neck, underarm, and groin can be felt by healthcare providers, potentially indicating disease involvement. This dual role—as a metastatic site and a clinical indicator—makes lymph nodes a critical entity in the assessment and staging of kidney cancer. The relationship between physical exam and lymph nodes highlights the clinical utility of this examination. [Data: Entities (43, 109); Relationships (56, 142)]

## The primary tumor and metastatic tumors are interconnected in disease progression

The primary tumor is the original tumor in the kidney from which cancer cells can spread. Metastatic tumors form when cancer cells from the primary tumor travel to distant sites. Understanding this relationship is essential for understanding the natural history of kidney cancer and for developing treatment strategies. The data explicitly links metastasis to both the primary tumor and metastatic tumors, emphasizing the continuum of disease progression. [Data: Entities (65, 64); Relationships (77, 76)]"

8|Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions|"# Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions

The community centers on Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC), a category of kidney cancers distinct from clear cell RCC. Key entities include various subtypes: papillary RCC (the most common), chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, collecting duct RCC, and renal medullary carcinoma. These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait and sickle cell disease, particularly in young people of African descent. Collecting duct RCC forms in the collecting ducts and is also known as cdRCC. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by chromophobe cells. The community highlights the diversity of NCCRCC and its connections to specific cellular features and genetic conditions.

## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

## The community highlights the importance of accurate subtyping for prognosis and treatment

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. The structured relationships in this community provide a framework for classifying and studying NCCRCC. [Data: Entities (27, 34, 21, 29, 32); Relationships (34, 42, 21, 37, 40, +more)]"

Kidney cancer tends to spread to distant sites such as the lungs, lymph nodes, and bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. Multiple tumors in one or both kidneys are not considered metastasis and are treated as separate primary tumors. Treatment will be based on the size, known or suspected subtype, and location of the tumor(s). Key points h The kidneys filter blood to remove extra water and other waste the body doesn’t need. Blood flows into the kidney through the renal artery and out through the renal vein. Renal tubules are tiny tubes in the kidneys that remove waste from blood and make urine. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) starts in cells that line the renal tubules. RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer and is the focus of the book. Clear cell RCC and non-clear cell RCC are subtypes. h Almost any type of RCC can become sarcomatoid (sRCC) or have sarcomatoid features. Tumors can grow in any part of the kidney and can grow into the renal vein and vena cava. Treatment for RCC is based on histology, tumor(s) size and location, and if cancer has metastasized to other areas in the body. 2 Diagnosing kidney cancer Test results General health tests Blood tests Urine tests Imaging tests Biopsy Biomarker testing Genetic risk testing Performance status Key points Most kidney cancers are found by chance during imaging tests for other health problems. Further testing is used to confirm (diagnose) kidney cancer. This chapter presents an overview of possible tests you might receive and what to expect. Test results Results from imaging studies and possible biopsy will be used to determine your treatment plan. Treatment will be based on these findings. It is important you understand what these tests mean. Ask questions about your test results. Don’t hesitate to ask questions and take notes during appointments. Write down questions and ask a friend or family member to take notes. Caregivers should ask questions, too. Organize your medical documents, including insurance forms, medical records, and test results. Keep a list of contact information for your care team and update your primary care physician (PCP) regarding any changes. Include details about the specific type of cancer, treatment, and dates in your contact list. Keep these things in mind: It's beneficial to have a support system in place during diagnosis and treatment. Enlist the help of friends, family members, or peers who can provide transportation, meals, and emotional support. These can be different people for different tasks or change over time. Consider bringing someone with you to doctor visits if possible or have someone on the phone or join you for telehealth visits. Ask your care team how best to communicate with them, especially in an emergency. For possible tests and procedures, see Guide
4| health history. You can ask family members about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. For relatives who have died, ask about the cause and age of death. Start by asking your parents, siblings, and children. Next, talk to half-siblings, aunts and uncles, niece and nephews, grandparents, and grandchildren. Write down what you learn about your family history and share this information with your health care provider. Some of the questions to ask include: Do you have any chronic diseases, such as heart disease or diabetes, or health conditions such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol? Have you had any other diseases, such as cancer or stroke? How old were you when each of these diseases and health conditions was diagnosed? What is our family’s ancestry—from what countries did our ancestors originate? Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting test images, will write a report and send this report to your doctor. Your test results will be discussed with you. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed three-dimensional (3D) picture. In most cases, contrast will be used. Contrast Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. Contrast is used to make the pictures clearer. It might be taken by mouth (oral) or given through a vein (IV). The contrast is not permanent and will leave the body in your urine after the test. The types of contrast vary but are different for CT than for MRI. Tell your doctors if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and prednisone (steroids), to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys are not working well. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Contrast might be used. An MRI may be used as an initial test, to check treatment results, and to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. PET scans are performed about an hour after the tracer is injected. PET scans are combined with CT or MRI scans (PET/CT or PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. This combined test is considered to be more accurate than either scan alone. Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. FDG-PET scans can help determine if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. SSTR-PET/CT scan A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) antagonist is a protein found on the surface of cells that bind to a hormone called somatostatin. Somatostatin helps to control other hormones in the body. SSTRs are found on many different types of cells. A SSTR-PET uses a tracer that binds to these SSTRs. Blood tests Blood tests are used to look for signs of hormone secretion or to see how well you are responding to certain treatments. Biochemical tests Biochemical tests measure substances like hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva that may be made by the adrenal tumor. Symptoms may be seen when your body makes too much of a hormone. Your doctor may consider these tests if you may have an adrenal tumor or syndromes caused by a tumor. More information on biochemical tests can be found in Guide Guide 1 Biochemical tests

question: How would you distinguish between a functional adenoma and a pheochromocytoma in a patient with an adrenal mass and high blood pressure?
pred_answer: A functional adenoma typically arises from the adrenal cortex and may cause Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess) or primary aldosteronism (aldosterone excess) with hypertension and possible hypokalemia, whereas a pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla and is characterized by high blood pressure along with headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating due to catecholamine release. Distinction is made through hormone testing (e.g., cortisol/aldosterone for adenoma; metanephrines/catecholamines for pheochromocytoma) and clinical presentation.

Thought: The question requires distinguishing between a functional adenoma and a pheochromocytoma based on the provided reports and data.  

1. **Identify key characteristics from the text**:  
   - **Functional adenoma**: Described as the most common adrenal tumor, noncancerous, can produce excess hormones. Specifically, an adenoma producing excess cortisol causes Cushing syndrome, and one producing excess aldosterone is called an aldosteronoma.  
   - **Pheochromocytoma**: Originates in the adrenal medulla, characterized by high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating; most are benign but can be cancerous.  

2. **Relate to clinical presentation**:  
   - High blood pressure is a symptom shared by both conditions—aldosteronoma (functional adenoma) causes hypertension via aldosterone excess, while pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal or sustained hypertension due to catecholamine release.  
   - However, pheochromocytoma is specifically linked with additional symptoms: headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating (the classic triad), which are not highlighted for functional adenomas.  
   - Functional adenomas may present with endocrine syndromes like Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess) or primary aldosteronism (aldosterone excess), which have distinct metabolic and electrolyte features (e.g., hypokalemia in aldosteronoma).  

3. **Diagnostic distinction**:  
   - Biochemical tests measuring hormones in blood/urine/saliva are used for adrenal tumors. For pheochromocytoma, measurement of metanephrines or catecholamines would be expected. For functional adenoma, cortisol or aldosterone levels would be assessed.  
   - Imaging may localize the tumor, but pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla, whereas adenomas arise from the adrenal cortex.  

4. **Conclusion**: Distinguish by clinical symptoms (presence of paroxysmal headache, palpitations, sweating suggests pheochromocytoma), hormone testing (catecholamines/metanephrines vs. cortisol/aldosterone), and tumor origin (medulla vs. cortex).  

Answer: A functional adenoma typically arises from the adrenal cortex and may cause Cushing syndrome (cortisol excess) or primary aldosteronism (aldosterone excess) with hypertension and possible hypokalemia, whereas a pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla and is characterized by high blood pressure along with headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating due to catecholamine release. Distinction is made through hormone testing (e.g., cortisol/aldosterone for adenoma; metanephrines/catecholamines for pheochromocytoma) and clinical presentation.

0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. It might be taken by mouth (oral) or given through a vein (IV). The contrast is not permanent and will leave the body in your urine after the test. The types of contrast vary but are different for CT than for MRI. Tell your doctors if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and prednisone (steroids), to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys are not working well. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Contrast might be used. An MRI may be used as an initial test, to check treatment results, and to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. PET scans are performed about an hour after the tracer is injected. PET scans are combined with CT or MRI scans (PET/CT or PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. This combined test is considered to be more accurate than either scan alone. Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. FDG-PET scans can help determine if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. SSTR-PET/CT scan A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) antagonist is a protein found on the surface of cells that bind to a hormone called somatostatin. Somatostatin helps to control other hormones in the body. SSTRs are found on many different types of cells. A SSTR-PET uses a tracer that binds to these SSTRs. Blood tests Blood tests are used to look for signs of hormone secretion or to see how well you are responding to certain treatments. Biochemical tests Biochemical tests measure substances like hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva that may be made by the adrenal tumor. Symptoms may be seen when your body makes too much of a hormone. Your doctor may consider these tests if you may have an adrenal tumor or syndromes caused by a tumor. pred_answer: Symptoms of hypertension and hypokalemia (with low renin) plus biochemical tests showing elevated aldosterone suggest an aldosteronoma, whereas features of Cushing syndrome (e.g., weight gain, muscle weakness, stretch marks) with elevated cortisol suggest a cortisol-producing adenoma.
raw_response:
Thought: To distinguish aldosteronoma from a cortisol-producing adenoma, the key is the specific hormone excess and its clinical effects. Aldosteronoma produces excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (e.g., hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin). A cortisol-producing adenoma causes Cushing syndrome (e.g., weight gain, muscle weakness, stretch marks, and elevated cortisol). Biochemical tests measuring aldosterone versus cortisol would confirm the diagnosis. Therefore, the combination is hypertension with hypokalemia and elevated aldosterone with suppressed renin for aldosteronoma, versus features of Cushing syndrome with elevated cortisol for a cortisol-producing adenoma.
Answer: Symptoms of hypertension and hypokalemia (with low renin) plus biochemical tests showing elevated aldosterone suggest an aldosteronoma, whereas features of Cushing syndrome (e.g., weight gain, muscle weakness, stretch marks) with elevated cortisol suggest a cortisol-producing adenoma.

0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

## Overlap between hereditary syndrome entities

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. This redundancy reinforces the importance of these syndromes in the community. [Data: Entities (96, 78, 98, 81, 99, 82, 100, 83); Relationships (114, 95, 116, 98, 117, 99, 118, 100)]"

What is our family’s ancestry—from what countries did our ancestors originate? Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting test images, will write a report and send this report to your doctor. Your test results will be discussed with you. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed three-dimensional (3D) picture. In most cases, contrast will be used. Contrast Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. Contrast is used to make the pictures clearer. It might be taken by mouth (oral) or given through a vein (IV). The contrast is not permanent and will leave the body in your urine after the test. The types of contrast vary but are different for CT than for MRI. Tell your doctors if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and prednisone (steroids), to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys are not working well. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Contrast might be used. An MRI may be used as an initial test, to check treatment results, and to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. This combined test is considered to be more accurate than either scan alone. Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. Biochemical tests Biochemical tests measure substances like hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva that may be made by the adrenal tumor. Symptoms may be seen when your body makes too much of a hormone. Your doctor may consider these tests if you may have an adrenal tumor or syndromes caused by a tumor. question: What are the major subtypes of kidney cancer and how are they histologically classified?
pred_answer:
The major subtypes of kidney cancer are primarily classified under renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which accounts for about 90% of kidney cancers. RCC subtypes are histologically classified by examining cancer cells under a microscope (histology). The key subtypes are:
- Clear cell RCC (ccRCC): the most common subtype (~70% of RCC cases); cells appear very pale or clear under a microscope.
- Non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC): includes several subtypes:
  - Papillary RCC: most common nccRCC subtype (~10% of RCC cases); tumors typically look like long, thin, finger-like growths.
  - Chromophobe RCC: cells are pale but larger than clear cells and look different.
  - Translocation RCC: tumors have unique gene fusions.
  - Unclassified RCC: cancer cells don't look like any subtype or more than one subtype is present.
  - Rare types: collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma.
- Recently defined RCC types: clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC.
- Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC): not a distinct subtype but a transformation that can arise from almost any RCC type; occurs in <5% of RCC tumors, with cells resembling sarcoma cells.
Other less common kidney cancers include urothelial carcinoma (starts in the renal pelvis and ureter lining, sharing features with bladder cancer), Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma, usually in young children), and renal sarcoma (starts in blood vessels or connective tissue).

7|Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network|"# Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network

This community centers on renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, and its metastatic spread. Key entities include RCC, its sarcomatoid variant (sRCC), various subtypes (ccRCC, clear cell papillary RCC, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, ELOC-mutated RCC), and distant sites of metastasis such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The relationships illustrate how RCC can transform into sarcomatoid RCC, how metastasis occurs to these sites, and how physical exams can detect lymph node involvement.

## RCC is the most common kidney cancer with high metastatic potential

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, originating in the renal tubules. It has a high propensity to metastasize, as evidenced by multiple relationships linking RCC to distant sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The centrality of RCC is underscored by its high degree (8) and its connections to various subtypes. The metastatic capability makes RCC a significant clinical challenge, as early detection and treatment are critical for patient outcomes. [Data: Entities (25, 48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46); Relationships (49, 56, 55, 57, 58, 59)]

## Sarcomatoid RCC is an aggressive variant arising from any RCC subtype

Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) is a highly aggressive form of kidney cancer that can arise from almost any type of RCC, as indicated by the relationship between sRCC and RCC. This transformation is associated with a worse prognosis and increased likelihood of metastasis. sRCC occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors but tends to grow and spread more rapidly. The entity 'SRCC' is synonymous with sarcomatoid RCC, highlighting the importance of recognizing this variant due to its clinical implications. [Data: Entities (39, 40); Relationships (47, 48)]

## Metastasis is a central process involving multiple distant sites

Metastasis is a key process in kidney cancer progression, where cancer cells travel through blood or lymph to form new tumors outside the kidney. The data reveals that RCC commonly metastasizes to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. This pattern of spread guides staging and treatment decisions. The high degree of the metastasis entity (9) and its numerous relationships underscore its critical role in the disease. [Data: Entities (48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46, 64); Relationships (56, 55, 57, 58, 59, 76)]

## Clear cell RCC is the most common subtype, with several recently defined subtypes

Clear cell RCC (ccRCC) is the predominant subtype of RCC, accounting for about 70% of cases. Additionally, several recently defined RCC types have been identified, including clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC. These subtypes have distinct molecular and pathological features that may influence prognosis and treatment. The relationships show that these subtypes are all connected to RCC, indicating their classification within the broader RCC spectrum. [Data: Entities (26, 36, 37, 38); Relationships (33, 44, 45, 46)]

## Lymph nodes are key sites for metastasis and physical examination

Lymph nodes serve as an important site for kidney cancer metastasis and are also accessible during physical exams. Enlarged lymph nodes in areas such as the neck, underarm, and groin can be felt by healthcare providers, potentially indicating disease involvement. This dual role—as a metastatic site and a clinical indicator—makes lymph nodes a critical entity in the assessment and staging of kidney cancer. The relationship between physical exam and lymph nodes highlights the clinical utility of this examination. [Data: Entities (43, 109); Relationships (56, 142)]

## The primary tumor and metastatic tumors are interconnected in disease progression

The primary tumor is the original tumor in the kidney from which cancer cells can spread. Metastatic tumors form when cancer cells from the primary tumor travel to distant sites. Understanding this relationship is essential for understanding the natural history of kidney cancer and for developing treatment strategies. The data explicitly links metastasis to both the primary tumor and metastatic tumors, emphasizing the continuum of disease progression. [Data: Entities (65, 64); Relationships (77, 76)]"

7|Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network|"# Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) and Metastasis Network

This community centers on renal cell carcinoma (RCC), the most common type of kidney cancer, and its metastatic spread. Key entities include RCC, its sarcomatoid variant (sRCC), various subtypes (ccRCC, clear cell papillary RCC, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, ELOC-mutated RCC), and distant sites of metastasis such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The relationships illustrate how RCC can transform into sarcomatoid RCC, how metastasis occurs to these sites, and how physical exams can detect lymph node involvement.

## RCC is the most common kidney cancer with high metastatic potential

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, originating in the renal tubules. It has a high propensity to metastasize, as evidenced by multiple relationships linking RCC to distant sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, bones, liver, and brain. The centrality of RCC is underscored by its high degree (8) and its connections to various subtypes. The metastatic capability makes RCC a significant clinical challenge, as early detection and treatment are critical for patient outcomes. [Data: Entities (25, 48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46); Relationships (49, 56, 55, 57, 58, 59)]

## Sarcomatoid RCC is an aggressive variant arising from any RCC subtype

Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) is a highly aggressive form of kidney cancer that can arise from almost any type of RCC, as indicated by the relationship between sRCC and RCC. This transformation is associated with a worse prognosis and increased likelihood of metastasis. sRCC occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors but tends to grow and spread more rapidly. The entity 'SRCC' is synonymous with sarcomatoid RCC, highlighting the importance of recognizing this variant due to its clinical implications. [Data: Entities (39, 40); Relationships (47, 48)]

## Metastasis is a central process involving multiple distant sites

Metastasis is a key process in kidney cancer progression, where cancer cells travel through blood or lymph to form new tumors outside the kidney. The data reveals that RCC commonly metastasizes to lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. This pattern of spread guides staging and treatment decisions. The high degree of the metastasis entity (9) and its numerous relationships underscore its critical role in the disease. [Data: Entities (48, 43, 42, 44, 45, 46, 64); Relationships (56, 55, 57, 58, 59, 76)]

## Clear cell RCC is the most common subtype, with several recently defined subtypes

Clear cell RCC (ccRCC) is the predominant subtype of RCC, accounting for about 70% of cases. Additionally, several recently defined RCC types have been identified, including clear cell papillary renal cell tumor, fumarate hydratase-deficient RCC, and ELOC-mutated RCC. These subtypes have distinct molecular and pathological features that may influence prognosis and treatment. The relationships show that these subtypes are all connected to RCC, indicating their classification within the broader RCC spectrum. [Data: Entities (26, 36, 37, 38); Relationships (33, 44, 45, 46)]

## Lymph nodes are key sites for metastasis and physical examination

Lymph nodes serve as an important site for kidney cancer metastasis and are also accessible during physical exams. Enlarged lymph nodes in areas such as the neck, underarm, and groin can be felt by healthcare providers, potentially indicating disease involvement. This dual role—as a metastatic site and a clinical indicator—makes lymph nodes a critical entity in the assessment and staging of kidney cancer. The relationship between physical exam and lymph nodes highlights the clinical utility of this examination. [Data: Entities (43, 109); Relationships (56, 142)]

## The primary tumor and metastatic tumors are interconnected in disease progression

The primary tumor is the original tumor in the kidney from which cancer cells can spread. Metastatic tumors form when cancer cells from the primary tumor travel to distant sites. Understanding this relationship is essential for understanding the natural history of kidney cancer and for developing treatment strategies. The data explicitly links metastasis to both the primary tumor and metastatic tumors, emphasizing the continuum of disease progression. [Data: Entities (65, 64); Relationships (77, 76)]"

The renal tubules remove waste and other substances from the blood. These substances are made into urine. The clean, filtered blood flows out of the kidney through the renal vein. The renal vein merges with a larger vein called the vena cava. The vena cava takes clean blood back up to the heart. question: What are the main types of adrenal tumors and how do they differ in terms of malignancy and function?
pred_answer: The main types of adrenal tumors include adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), neuroblastoma, and pheochromocytoma. Adenoma is the most common, typically noncancerous (benign) but can be functional, producing excess hormones such as cortisol (causing Cushing syndrome) or aldosterone (aldosteronoma). Adrenocortical carcinoma is a rare malignant cancer that can be functioning or nonfunctioning and may produce multiple hormones. Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous tumor affecting children, often spreading to other parts of the body. Pheochromocytoma begins in the adrenal medulla, is usually benign but can be cancerous, and is characterized by high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating. In general, adrenal tumors can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally.
