0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

## Overlap between hereditary syndrome entities

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. This redundancy reinforces the importance of these syndromes in the community. [Data: Entities (96, 78, 98, 81, 99, 82, 100, 83); Relationships (114, 95, 116, 98, 117, 99, 118, 100)]"

0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

## Overlap between hereditary syndrome entities

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. This redundancy reinforces the importance of these syndromes in the community. [Data: Entities (96, 78, 98, 81, 99, 82, 100, 83); Relationships (114, 95, 116, 98, 117, 99, 118, 100)]"

PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. PET scans are performed about an hour after the tracer is injected. PET scans are combined with CT or MRI scans (PET/CT or PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. Adrenal glands produce hormones that affect your body in different ways. This chapter reviews the basics of adrenal tumors. Adrenal glands Your body has 2 adrenal glands. They are located on top of each kidney. Adrenal glands are small, yellow glands that are important to the body’s endocrine system. The endocrine system is made up of tissues and organs that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These hormones control metabolism, blood pressure, and body features (such as hair growth and body shape). Adrenal medulla – This is the inner part of the adrenal gland. The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. Adrenal glands Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. Multiple tumors in one or both kidneys are not considered metastasis and are treated as separate primary tumors. Treatment will be based on the size, known or suspected subtype, and location of the tumor(s). Key points h The kidneys filter blood to remove extra water and other waste the body doesn’t need. Blood flows into the kidney through the renal artery and out through the renal vein. Renal tubules are tiny tubes in the kidneys that remove waste from blood and make urine. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) starts in cells that line the renal tubules. RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer and is the focus of the book. Clear cell RCC and non-clear cell RCC are subtypes. h Almost any type of RCC can become sarcomatoid (sRCC) or have sarcomatoid features. Tumors can grow in any part of the kidney and can grow into the renal vein and vena cava. Treatment for RCC is based on histology, tumor(s) size and location, and if cancer has metastasized to other areas in the body. 2 Diagnosing kidney cancer Test results General health tests Blood tests Urine tests Imaging tests Biopsy Biomarker testing Genetic risk testing Performance status Key points Most kidney cancers are found by chance during imaging tests for other health problems. 0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

## Overlap between hereditary syndrome entities

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. This redundancy reinforces the importance of these syndromes in the community. [Data: Entities (96, 78, 98, 81, 99, 82, 100, 83); Relationships (114, 95, 116, 98, 117, 99, 118, 100)]"

Dear Multidisciplinary Tumor Board,

I am referring a 62-year-old patient recently diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma (RCC) exhibiting sarcomatoid features and suspected lung metastases for your expert review and management recommendations.

**Case Summary:**  
The patient is a 62-year-old individual who presented with a renal mass. Diagnostic imaging revealed a kidney tumor, and subsequent biopsy confirmed RCC with sarcomatoid features. Further workup, including chest imaging, is suspicious for pulmonary metastases.

**Diagnostic Findings:**  
- Imaging: Renal mass identified on CT/MRI; chest imaging shows findings concerning for lung metastases.  
- Biopsy: Histopathology demonstrates RCC with sarcomatoid features, meaning the cancer cells resemble sarcoma cells.  
- No definitive subtype specified, but sarcomatoid transformation can occur in any RCC subtype.

**Histology:**  
Sarcomatoid RCC (sRCC) is not a distinct subtype but a transformation that can arise from almost any RCC subtype. It occurs in less than 5% of RCC tumors but is associated with aggressive behavior, rapid growth, and increased likelihood of metastasis. The presence of sarcomatoid features often indicates a poorer prognosis.

**Staging:**  
Given suspected lung metastases, the disease is likely stage IV (metastatic). Kidney cancer commonly spreads to distant sites such as the lungs, bones, and lymph nodes. The sarcomatoid component further increases metastatic potential.

**Key Considerations for Management:**  
1. **Aggressive Biology:** Sarcomatoid RCC tends to grow quickly and spread, making treatment challenging.  
2. **Systemic Therapy:** Given metastatic disease, systemic therapies (e.g., immune checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors) should be considered. Clinical trials may be appropriate.  
3. **Multidisciplinary Approach:** Input from medical oncology, urology, radiology, and pathology is essential.  
4. **Prognosis:** Sarcomatoid features and lung metastases portend a poor prognosis; timely intervention is critical.  
5. **Supportive Care:** Symptom management and quality of life should be prioritized.

I would appreciate your recommendations regarding systemic therapy options, potential clinical trials, and any additional staging or molecular testing that may guide treatment.

Thank you for your expertise.

Sincerely,  
[Urologist’s Name]

The community centers on Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC), a category of kidney cancers distinct from clear cell RCC. Key entities include various subtypes: papillary RCC (the most common), chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, collecting duct RCC, and renal medullary carcinoma. These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. ## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. question: You are an oncologist tasked with drafting an initial treatment plan for a patient newly diagnosed with non-clear cell RCC (papillary subtype) confined to the kidney, with no evidence of metastasis. Outline your diagnostic confirmation, staging, and treatment strategy.
pred_answer: Confirm diagnosis with pathology review and imaging; stage with abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI plus chest imaging to document localized disease; treat with surgical resection, preferably partial nephrectomy if feasible, otherwise radical nephrectomy, with surveillance afterward and no routine systemic therapy for non-metastatic disease.
raw_response:
Thought: The patient has non-clear cell RCC, specifically papillary subtype, confined to the kidney with no metastasis, so this is localized disease. Diagnostic confirmation should include histologic review to confirm papillary RCC and exclude other NCCRCC subtypes; imaging with CT or MRI of the abdomen/pelvis is needed, and staging should assess local extent, renal vein/vena cava involvement, Gerota’s fascia invasion, lymph nodes, and distant sites, typically with chest imaging. Treatment strategy for localized papillary RCC is primarily surgical, with partial nephrectomy preferred when feasible for confined tumors, otherwise radical nephrectomy; lymph node dissection may be considered if suspicious nodes are present. Systemic therapy is not standard for localized disease without metastasis, but accurate subtyping and pathology review are important because papillary RCC can have variable behavior, and adjuvant therapy is generally not routine outside clinical trials. Surveillance after surgery is appropriate, with imaging and clinical follow-up based on stage and risk.
Answer: Confirm diagnosis with pathology review and imaging; stage with abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI plus chest imaging to document localized disease; treat with surgical resection, preferably partial nephrectomy if feasible, otherwise radical nephrectomy, with surveillance afterward and no routine systemic therapy for non-metastatic disease.

8|Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions|"# Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions

The community centers on Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC), a category of kidney cancers distinct from clear cell RCC. Key entities include various subtypes: papillary RCC (the most common), chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, collecting duct RCC, and renal medullary carcinoma. These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait and sickle cell disease, particularly in young people of African descent. Collecting duct RCC forms in the collecting ducts and is also known as cdRCC. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by chromophobe cells. The community highlights the diversity of NCCRCC and its connections to specific cellular features and genetic conditions.

## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

## The community highlights the importance of accurate subtyping for prognosis and treatment

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. The structured relationships in this community provide a framework for classifying and studying NCCRCC. [Data: Entities (27, 34, 21, 29, 32); Relationships (34, 42, 21, 37, 40, +more)]"

**DISCHARGE SUMMARY**

**Patient Name:** [Redacted]  
**Date of Admission:** [Redacted]  
**Date of Discharge:** [Redacted]  
**Diagnosis:** Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) of the right kidney, locally advanced without distant metastasis.

**Presenting History:**  
The patient is an adult with newly diagnosed kidney cancer. Diagnostic imaging revealed a renal mass. Biopsy and histopathological examination confirmed clear cell RCC, the most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 7 out of 10 people with RCC. Under microscopy, clear cells appear pale or clear. The tumor originates in the cells lining the renal tubules.

**Hospital Course:**  
Staging evaluation demonstrated local extension of the tumor into surrounding tissues, including nearby fat, blood vessels, lymph nodes, adrenal glands, and/or Gerota’s fascia. There is no evidence of distant metastasis to the lungs, lymph nodes, bones, liver, or brain. The disease is classified as locally advanced (Stage III), not metastatic. No sarcomatoid features were identified. Renal function and overall clinical status remained stable during admission.

**Subtype and Staging:**  
- Subtype: Clear cell RCC (ccRCC)  
- Local spread: Present (invasion of nearby structures such as Gerota’s fascia, renal vein, or perinephric fat)  
- Distant metastasis: Absent  
- Sarcomatoid features: Not identified  

**Treatment Plan:**  
Treatment will be based on tumor size, location, and histology. Given local extension without distant metastasis, surgical resection (e.g., radical nephrectomy) is planned, with consideration of adjuvant therapy as appropriate. No systemic therapy for metastatic disease is indicated at this time.

**Discharge Medications:**  
- Analgesics as prescribed for postoperative pain (if applicable)  
- Antiemetics as needed  
- No chemotherapy or targeted therapy at discharge  

**Follow-Up:**  
- Surgical oncology and urology clinic in 2–4 weeks for wound check and treatment planning  
- Medical oncology referral for surveillance and consideration of adjuvant therapy  
- Repeat imaging (CT or MRI) in 3–6 months to monitor for recurrence or distant metastasis  

**Discharge Instructions:**  
- Monitor for fever, worsening pain, hematuria, or wound drainage  
- Maintain adequate hydration and follow a renal-friendly diet  
- Avoid strenuous activity for 4–6 weeks post-surgery  
- Report any new bone pain, cough, or neurological symptoms immediately, as these may indicate distant spread  
- Keep all follow-up appointments and maintain a medical binder with test results and records

8|Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions|"# Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC) Subtypes and Associated Conditions

The community centers on Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (NCCRCC), a category of kidney cancers distinct from clear cell RCC. Key entities include various subtypes: papillary RCC (the most common), chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, collecting duct RCC, and renal medullary carcinoma. These subtypes are linked to NCCRCC through subtype relationships. Papillary RCC is further characterized by papillary tumors and is also known as PRCC. Renal medullary carcinoma is strongly associated with sickle cell trait and sickle cell disease, particularly in young people of African descent. Collecting duct RCC forms in the collecting ducts and is also known as cdRCC. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by chromophobe cells. The community highlights the diversity of NCCRCC and its connections to specific cellular features and genetic conditions.

## NCCRCC encompasses a diverse group of kidney cancer subtypes

Non-clear cell RCC (NCCRCC) is a broad category of renal cell carcinoma that includes several distinct subtypes, each with unique characteristics. The most common subtype is papillary RCC, which accounts for a significant portion of NCCRCC cases. Other subtypes include chromophobe RCC, translocation RCC, unclassified RCC, and rare types such as collecting duct RCC and renal medullary carcinoma. This diversity underscores the complexity of diagnosing and treating NCCRCC, as each subtype may have different clinical behaviors and treatment responses. The relationships among these entities highlight the hierarchical structure of NCCRCC classification. [Data: Entities (27, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34); Relationships (34, 42, 40, 37, 38, 39, +more)]

## Papillary RCC is the predominant subtype of NCCRCC

Papillary RCC is identified as the most common subtype of non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma, occurring in approximately 1 out of every 10 people diagnosed with RCC. It is characterized by a distinctive microscopic appearance, with tumors resembling long, thin, finger-like growths. Papillary RCC is also known by the alternative name PRCC. The prominence of papillary RCC within NCCRCC makes it a key focus for research and clinical management. Its relationship to papillary tumors further defines its morphological features. [Data: Entities (21, 28, 59); Relationships (21, 36, 70)]

## Renal medullary carcinoma is a rare but aggressive subtype linked to sickle cell conditions

Renal medullary carcinoma (RMC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that predominantly affects young people of African descent who carry the sickle cell trait or have sickle cell disease. These conditions can cause sickling of red blood cells, which is associated with the development of RMC. The strong association with sickle cell trait and disease highlights the importance of genetic and ethnic factors in this subtype. RMC is also known by the abbreviation RMC. Its rarity and aggressive nature make it a critical area of study. [Data: Entities (34, 35, 61, 62); Relationships (42, 43, 72, 73)]

## Chromophobe RCC is characterized by distinct cellular features

Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that is defined by the presence of chromophobe cells, which are pale but larger than clear cells and appear different under a microscope. This distinct cellular morphology aids in the diagnosis of chromophobe RCC. As a subtype of NCCRCC, it contributes to the heterogeneity of the disease. The relationship between chromophobe RCC and chromophobe cells underscores the importance of histopathological examination in classifying RCC subtypes. [Data: Entities (29, 60); Relationships (37, 71)]

## Collecting duct RCC is a rare subtype originating in the kidney's collecting ducts

Collecting duct RCC (cdRCC) is a rare type of NCCRCC that forms in the cells of the collecting ducts or tubules within the kidney. This subtype is also known as cdRCC. Its origin in the collecting ducts distinguishes it from other RCC subtypes. The relationship between collecting duct RCC and collecting ducts highlights the specific anatomical site of tumor development. Due to its rarity, collecting duct RCC poses diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. [Data: Entities (32, 33, 63); Relationships (40, 41, 74)]

## Translocation RCC and unclassified RCC are additional subtypes with unique characteristics

Translocation RCC is a subtype of NCCRCC that can occur at all ages but tends to be diagnosed in children or younger adults. It is characterized by unique fusions of genes that promote cancer. Unclassified RCC describes cancer cells that do not resemble any of the defined subtypes or where more than one subtype is present. These subtypes add to the complexity of NCCRCC and require specialized diagnostic approaches. Their relationships to NCCRCC are explicitly defined, emphasizing the comprehensive nature of the NCCRCC category. [Data: Entities (30, 31); Relationships (38, 39)]

## The community highlights the importance of accurate subtyping for prognosis and treatment

The diverse subtypes of NCCRCC have different clinical behaviors, prognoses, and treatment options. Accurate subtyping is crucial for determining the most appropriate management strategy. For example, renal medullary carcinoma is associated with a poor prognosis, while papillary RCC may have a more variable course. Understanding the relationships among subtypes and their associated conditions, such as sickle cell trait, can inform screening and early detection efforts. The structured relationships in this community provide a framework for classifying and studying NCCRCC. [Data: Entities (27, 34, 21, 29, 32); Relationships (34, 42, 21, 37, 40, +more)]"

question: Imagine you are an endocrinologist receiving a referral for a 45-year-old patient with an incidentally discovered adrenal mass on CT scan. Draft a detailed diagnostic workup plan, integrating risk assessment for malignancy and hormone excess, as recommended by the guidelines.
pred_answer:
Diagnostic workup plan for a 45-year-old with incidental adrenal mass:

1. **Initial assessment**: Review CT scan for size, density, margins, homogeneity, and contrast enhancement. Most incidental adrenal masses are benign adenomas (<4 cm, homogeneous, low density). Note any suspicious features (size >4 cm, irregular margins, heterogeneity, necrosis, calcifications).

2. **Hormone excess evaluation** (functional assessment):
   - **Cortisol excess**: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol. If abnormal, consider Cushing syndrome.
   - **Aldosterone excess**: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity (aldosterone-to-renin ratio) if hypertension or hypokalemia.
   - **Catecholamine excess**: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines if symptoms (headache, palpitations, sweating, hypertension) suggest pheochromocytoma.
   - **Androgen excess**: DHEA-S, testosterone if virilization or hirsutism.
   - **Biochemical tests**: Measure hormones in blood, urine, or saliva as indicated.

3. **Malignancy risk assessment**:
   - Imaging: If CT features are indeterminate or size >4 cm, consider MRI or FDG-PET/CT. FDG-PET can help differentiate benign from malignant; SSTR-PET if neuroendocrine tumor suspected.
   - Biopsy: Not routinely recommended for adrenal masses; consider if metastasis or infection suspected, or if imaging is inconclusive and results would change management.
   - Genetic testing: If family history or clinical features suggest hereditary syndrome (e.g., MEN1, MEN2, VHL, NF1, Lynch, Li-Fraumeni, FAP, Carney complex, Beckwith-Wiedemann, PGL/PCC), refer for genetic counseling and testing.

4. **Additional workup**:
   - Medical history and family history to assess risk for hereditary syndromes and guide testing.
   - Physical exam for signs of hormone excess (e.g., Cushingoid features, hypertension, virilization).
   - Blood tests for general health and hormone levels.
   - If functional tumor confirmed, additional imaging (e.g., adrenal vein sampling for aldosteronoma) and referral to endocrinology/surgery.

5. **Follow-up and management**:
   - If nonfunctional and benign imaging features: Follow-up imaging in 6–12 months to assess stability.
   - If functional or suspicious for malignancy: Refer to surgery, oncology, or multidisciplinary team. Consider adrenalectomy if indicated.
   - Genetic counseling if hereditary syndrome suspected.

This plan integrates guidelines from NCCN and addresses both hormone excess and malignancy risk, using imaging, biochemical, and genetic tests as appropriate.

0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

0|Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes|"# Adrenal Tumors and Associated Hereditary Syndromes

The community centers on adrenal tumors, which are tumors that form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant. A key entity is adenoma, the most common type of adrenal tumor, which is noncancerous but can be functional. Numerous hereditary conditions, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. Additionally, neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor affecting children. Some hereditary conditions also increase the risk of kidney tumors. Functional adenomas can lead to conditions like Cushing syndrome and aldosteronoma. Genetic testing is used for diagnosis and treatment planning. The community is structured around these entities and their relationships, highlighting the genetic and clinical associations with adrenal tumors.

## Adrenal tumors as the central entity

Adrenal tumors are the core entity in this community, with a high degree of 27 connections to other entities. They form in the adrenal glands and can be benign or malignant, functional or nonfunctioning, with most being benign and often found incidentally. The centrality of adrenal tumors is evident from numerous relationships linking them to hereditary syndromes, other tumor types, and diagnostic procedures. This underscores their significance in the community's structure and the potential health impact. [Data: Entities (69); Relationships (80, 87, 90, 93, 94, +more)]

## Adenoma as the most common adrenal tumor

Adenoma, also known as adrenocortical adenoma, is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, being noncancerous and potentially functioning. It is directly linked to adrenal tumors and can cause conditions like Cushing syndrome when producing excess cortisol. Aldosteronoma, a specific type of adenoma, produces excess aldosterone. The prominence of adenoma in the community is highlighted by its relationships and its role in endocrine disorders. [Data: Entities (74, 75, 71); Relationships (87, 88, 89)]

## Hereditary syndromes increasing adrenal tumor risk

A significant number of hereditary conditions are associated with an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors. These include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1), multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Each of these syndromes has a documented relationship to adrenal tumors, indicating a genetic predisposition that is crucial for understanding the etiology and screening of adrenal tumors. [Data: Entities (76, 77, 79, 80, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101); Relationships (93, 94, 96, 97, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119)]

## Neuroblastoma as a rare pediatric adrenal tumor

Neuroblastoma is a rare cancerous adrenal tumor that primarily affects children ages 5 and under, most often found in infants, and can spread to other parts of the body including bones. It is distinct from the more common benign adenomas and represents a severe form of adrenal tumor with significant impact on pediatric health. Its relationship to adrenal tumors highlights the diversity of tumor types within the community. [Data: Entities (72); Relationships (90)]

## Association with kidney tumors

Some hereditary conditions that increase the risk of adrenal tumors also predispose individuals to kidney tumors. Specifically, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to an increased risk of developing kidney tumors, as indicated by a relationship between the syndrome and kidney tumor. This cross-organ risk underscores the systemic nature of these genetic syndromes and the need for comprehensive surveillance. [Data: Entities (76, 105); Relationships (120)]

## Functional adrenal tumors and endocrine syndromes

Adrenal tumors can be functional, meaning they produce excess hormones, leading to specific clinical syndromes. Adenomas that produce too much cortisol cause Cushing syndrome, while aldosteronomas produce excess aldosterone, leading to primary aldosteronism (not explicitly named but implied by the term aldosteronoma). These functional tumors are important because they cause distinct endocrine disorders that require targeted management. [Data: Entities (71, 75); Relationships (88, 89)]

## Genetic testing for diagnosis and treatment planning

Genetic tests are employed to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This highlights the role of genetic evaluation in the management of adrenal tumors, especially given the numerous hereditary syndromes associated with increased risk. The relationship between adrenal tumors and genetic tests indicates that molecular diagnostics are integral to personalized care. [Data: Entities (106); Relationships (139)]

## Overlap between hereditary syndrome entities

Several hereditary syndromes are represented by multiple entities with slightly different names, such as 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)' and 'FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS', as well as 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1 (MEN 1)' and 'MULTIPLE ENDOCRINE NEOPLASIA TYPE 1'. These duplicates suggest variations in naming or granularity in the data, but they all point to the same underlying conditions and their association with adrenal tumors. This redundancy reinforces the importance of these syndromes in the community. [Data: Entities (96, 78, 98, 81, 99, 82, 100, 83); Relationships (114, 95, 116, 98, 117, 99, 118, 100)]"

**Discharge Summary – Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC)**

**Presentation:**  
Patient presented with signs and symptoms consistent with adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), a rare adrenal cancer originating in the adrenal cortex. ACC is the most common type of adrenal gland cancer, affecting approximately 1–2 per million people, and can occur at any age, though it is most likely in children ages 5 and under and adults in their 40s and 50s. Half of patients experience symptoms from hormone overproduction (functional tumor), while others have symptoms due to tumor mass effect. Reported symptoms may include weight gain, muscle weakness, pink or purple stretch marks, hormonal changes (excess facial hair, hair loss, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, shrinking testicles), nausea, vomiting, abdominal bloating, back pain, fever, loss of appetite, and unintended weight loss. The tumor may be functioning or nonfunctioning and can produce more than one hormone.

**Diagnostic Process:**  
Diagnosis was established through a series of tests as per guideline recommendations. Medical and family histories were obtained to assess for hereditary risk factors. Physical exam evaluated for palpable masses, organ size, and lymphadenopathy. Imaging tests (CT, MRI, and/or PET scans such as FDG-PET or SSTR-PET) were used to visualize the adrenal tumor and assess for local invasion or metastasis. Blood and biochemical tests measured hormone levels to determine functionality. Genetic tests were employed to identify hereditary syndromes associated with increased ACC risk. Biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis of ACC. Treatment planning was based on these test results.

**Risk Assessment:**  
The patient’s risk for ACC was evaluated in the context of hereditary conditions. Several genetic syndromes are linked to an increased risk of developing adrenal tumors, including Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, Carney complex, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma (PGL/PCC) syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia types 1 and 2 (MEN 1, MEN 2), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL). Some of these conditions also predispose to kidney tumors. Family history was reviewed to help determine risk and guide treatment. Genetic testing was used to identify any underlying hereditary syndrome.

**Follow-up Recommendations:**  
Follow-up should be individualized based on treatment received, tumor functionality, and presence of hereditary syndromes. Regular surveillance is recommended to monitor for recurrence or progression, as cure is less likely if ACC has spread beyond the adrenal glands. Follow-up may include periodic imaging tests (CT/MRI/PET) and biochemical tests to monitor hormone levels. Genetic counseling and testing should be offered to family members if a hereditary syndrome is identified. Patients should be advised to maintain a medical binder with test results and contact information for their care team. Refer to the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Adrenal Tumors, 2022, for detailed surveillance protocols.

Adrenal glands produce hormones that affect your body in different ways. This chapter reviews the basics of adrenal tumors. Adrenal glands Your body has 2 adrenal glands. They are located on top of each kidney. Adrenal glands are small, yellow glands that are important to the body’s endocrine system. The endocrine system is made up of tissues and organs that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These hormones control metabolism, blood pressure, and body features (such as hair growth and body shape). Adrenal medulla – This is the inner part of the adrenal gland. The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. Adrenal glands Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. AnatomyoftheAdrenalGland Adrenal tumors Adrenal tumors can occur in one or both adrenal glands. Most adrenal gland tumors are benign (not cancer). Adrenal tumors often do not cause symptoms and are found through an imaging test such as a CT or MRI scan performed for another reason. Adrenal tumors are categorized in the following ways: Benign (not cancer) adrenal tumors do not metastasize (spread) to other parts of the body. This type of tumor is often found by chance through imaging tests done for an unrelated issue. Functional adrenal tumors are usually benign, although some are capable of becoming cancerous and spreading. Benign functional tumors can still produce hormones and may be found during tests for hormone-related symptoms. Malignant adrenal tumors are cancerous tumors. They are rare, with about 300 to 500 people being diagnosed each year. Certain genetic conditions may increase the risk for these tumors. treatment. An adenoma that produces too much of the hormone aldosterone is called an aldosteronoma. Whereas, an adenoma that produces too much of the hormone cortisol (stress hormone) causes a condition called Cushing syndrome. Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) – Although it is the most common type of adrenal gland cancer, it is very rare and affects approximately 1 to 2 people out of every 1 million. Adrenocortical carcinoma begins in the adrenal cortex. It can be a functioning or nonfunctioning tumor. If the tumor is functioning, it may produce more than 1 hormone. Neuroblastoma – This rare type of adrenal tumor is cancerous. It affects children ages 5 and under, though it is most often found in infants. Neuroblastoma can spread to other parts of the body, including the bones. Pheochromocytoma – This type of tumor begins in the adrenal medulla and is characterized by symptoms of high blood pressure, headache, rapid heartbeat, and sweating. Most pheochromocytomas are benign, but can be cancerous. Adenoma – This is the most common type of adrenal gland tumor, also referred to as adrenocortical adenoma. It is a noncancerous tumor that can be functioning or nonfunctioning. If an adenoma is small and/or does not produce excessive hormones, and is not causing symptoms, it may not need Types Adrenal tumor categories are further broken down into types. They include the following: Adrenocortical carcinoma Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is an adrenal cancer that starts in one or both of the adrenal glands. It can occur at any age. But it’s most likely to affect children ages 5 and under, and adults in their 40s and 50s. If caught early, adrenal cancer can be cured. However, if the cancer has spread beyond the adrenal glands, cure becomes less likely. Treatment can be used to delay progression or recurrence. Signs and symptoms Half of those with adrenal cancer will have symptoms caused by hormones produced by the tumor. Others may experience symptoms if the tumor has grown so large that it is pressing on nearby organs. If you have any of the signs or symptoms listed below, make sure to discuss them with your health care provider. Symptoms of adrenal cancer may include: Weight gain Muscle weakness Pink or purple stretch marks on the skin Hormonal changes such as excess facial hair, hair loss on the head, irregular periods, enlarged breast tissue, and shrinking testicles Nausea Vomiting Abdominal bloating Back pain Fever Loss of appetite Loss of weight without trying Risk factors There are no known causes for most adrenal tumors. However, some genetic (hereditary) conditions can put you at risk for developing an adrenal tumor. Hereditary conditions are mutations passed down from biological parent to child through genes. Testing is used to diagnose and plan treatment for adrenal tumors. This chapter presents an overview of the tests you might receive and what to expect. Test results Adrenal tumors will be diagnosed based on a series of test results. Your diagnosis will determine your treatment plan. It is important you understand what these tests mean. Keep these things in mind: Bring someone with you to doctor visits, if possible. Write down questions and take notes during appointments. Don’t be afraid to ask your care team questions. Get to know your care team and help them get to know you. Get copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about your specific disease. Organize your papers. Create files for insurance forms, medical records, and test results. You can do the same on your computer. Keep a list of contact information for everyone on your care team. Add it to your phone. Hang the list on your refrigerator or keep it in a place where someone can access it in an emergency. Keep your primary care physician informed of changes to this list. Create a medical binder A medical binder or notebook is a great way to organize all of your records in one place. Make copies of blood tests, imaging results, and reports about your specific type of cancer. It will be helpful when getting a second opinion. Choose a binder that meets your needs. Consider a zipper pocket to include a pen, small calendar, and insurance cards. Create folders for insurance forms, medical records, and tests results. You can do the same on your computer. Use online patient portals to view your test results and other records. Download or print the records to add to your binder. Organize your binder in a way that works for you. Add a section for questions and to take notes. Bring your medical binder to appointments. You never know when you might need it! General health tests Medical history A medical history is a record of all health issues and treatments you have had in your life. Be prepared to list any illness or injury and when it happened. Bring a list of old and new medicines and any over-the-counter medicines, herbals, or supplements you take. Tell your doctor about any symptoms you have. A medical or health history will help determine which treatment is best for you. Family history Some cancers and other diseases can run in families. Your doctor will ask about the health history of family members who are blood relatives. This information is called a family history. Ask family members about their health issues like heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, and at what age they were diagnosed. Physical exam During a physical exam, a health care provider may: Check your temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and breathing rate Check your weight and height Listen to your lungs and heart Look in your eyes, ears, nose, and throat Feel and apply pressure to parts of your body to see if organs are of normal size, are soft or hard, or cause pain when touched. Tell your doctor if you feel pain. Feel for enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, underarm, and groin. Tell your doctor if you have felt any lumps or have any pain. What is our family’s ancestry—from what countries did our ancestors originate? Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting test images, will write a report and send this report to your doctor. Your test results will be discussed with you. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed three-dimensional (3D) picture. In most cases, contrast will be used. Contrast Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. Contrast is used to make the pictures clearer. It might be taken by mouth (oral) or given through a vein (IV). The contrast is not permanent and will leave the body in your urine after the test. The types of contrast vary but are different for CT than for MRI. Tell your doctors if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and prednisone (steroids), to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys are not working well. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Contrast might be used. An MRI may be used as an initial test, to check treatment results, and to see if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to help see cancer cells in the body. PET scans are performed about an hour after the tracer is injected. PET scans are combined with CT or MRI scans (PET/CT or PET/MRI) to determine where the cancer cells are located. This combined test is considered to be more accurate than either scan alone. Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. FDG-PET scans can help determine if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. SSTR-PET/CT scan A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) antagonist is a protein found on the surface of cells that bind to a hormone called somatostatin. Somatostatin helps to control other hormones in the body. SSTRs are found on many different types of cells. A SSTR-PET uses a tracer that binds to these SSTRs. Blood tests Blood tests are used to look for signs of hormone secretion or to see how well you are responding to certain treatments. Biochemical tests Biochemical tests measure substances like hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva that may be made by the adrenal tumor. Symptoms may be seen when your body makes too much of a hormone. Your doctor may consider these tests if you may have an adrenal tumor or syndromes caused by a tumor. More information on biochemical tests can be found in Guide Guide 1 Biochemical tests

Sarcomatoid features Almost any type of renal cell carcinoma can become sarcomatoid (sRCC) or have sarcomatoid features. This means that the cells of the cancer look like the cells of a sarcoma (cancer of the connective tissues, such as muscles, nerves, fat, blood vessels, and fibrous tissue). Sarcomatoid renal cancers occur in less than of RCC tumors but when present tend to grow more quickly than other types of kidney cancer and are more likely to spread to other parts of the body. This makes them more difficult to treat. How kidney cancer spreads Tumors can grow in any part of the kidney and can grow into the renal vein and vena cava. Kidney cancer can also spread to other parts of the body in a process called metastasis. In metastasis, cancer cells travel through your blood or lymph to form new tumors outside of the kidney. The new tumors are called metastatic tumors or metastases. Local spread – In locally advanced disease, cancer has spread to a nearby area close to the primary tumor. Kidney cancer can invade nearby tissues like surrounding fat, blood vessels, lymph nodes, adrenal glands, and Gerota’s fascia. Distant metastasis – In metastatic disease, cancer has spread to distant parts of the body far from the primary site. Kidney cancer tends to spread to distant sites such as the lungs, lymph nodes, and bones, and less frequently to the liver and brain. Multiple tumors in one or both kidneys are not considered metastasis and are treated as separate primary tumors. Treatment will be based on the size, known or suspected subtype, and location of the tumor(s). Key points h The kidneys filter blood to remove extra water and other waste the body doesn’t need. Blood flows into the kidney through the renal artery and out through the renal vein. Renal tubules are tiny tubes in the kidneys that remove waste from blood and make urine. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) starts in cells that line the renal tubules. RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer and is the focus of the book. Clear cell RCC and non-clear cell RCC are subtypes. h Almost any type of RCC can become sarcomatoid (sRCC) or have sarcomatoid features. Tumors can grow in any part of the kidney and can grow into the renal vein and vena cava.
